main.title: Gears of War 3
main.summary: Gears of War 3 is a 2011 third-person shooter video game developed by Epic Games and published by Microsoft Studios for the Xbox 360.

cards.heading: The end of the original trilogy
cards.text: Gears of War 3 is a 2011 third-person shooter video game developed by Epic Games and published by Microsoft Studios for the Xbox 360. It is the third installment of the Gears of War series, and final game in the original trilogy. Originally due for release on April 8, 2011, the game was delayed and eventually released on September 20, 2011. The story was written by science fiction author Karen Traviss.

cards.heading: Cover, weapons and squad tactics
cards.text: Like its predecessors, Gears of War 3 is a third-person shooter that emphasizes the use of cover and squad tactics in order to survive combat situations. The player's character can carry four weapons: one pistol, one set of grenades, and two primary weapons. Firearms can be swapped with other weapons dropped by fallen foes or at stockpiles throughout the game, along with ammunition. New to Gears of War 3 is the ability to tag enemy opponents; computer-controlled allies will then concentrate fire on these marked enemies, while human allies will be alerted to their location on their HUD. Players can now also swap weapons and ammunition (and money during Horde Mode) with other allies in the course of battle.

cards.heading: Critical acclaim and a new chapter
cards.text: Like its predecessors, Gears of War 3 received widespread critical acclaim from critics. Critics praised its story, voice acting, visuals, and music, but criticized its lack of innovation. A sequel titled Gears of War 4, developed by The Coalition, was released in 2016.

main.title: Dark Souls
main.subtitle: Learning Lordran
main.summary: Released on September 22, 2011, Dark Souls made exploration, deliberate combat and learning from failure central to its journey through Lordran.

cards.heading: Learning the routes through Lordran
cards.text: Dark Souls was released for PlayStation 3 in Japan on September 22, 2011, before its North American and European releases in October. FromSoftware built Lordran as a connected world that players gradually learn through exploration and repeated attempts. Progress depends on recognizing routes, enemies and the consequences of earlier decisions, as well as developing the character. Director Hidetaka Miyazaki emphasized the freedom to overcome difficulty through different strategies rather than quick reactions alone. Exploration, combat and encounters with other players all contribute to that process.

cards.heading: Why a shortcut matters
cards.text: A door, ladder or passage can connect an unfamiliar area to somewhere already visited. Such shortcuts shorten future journeys and reveal how apparently distant places fit together. The player learns Lordran's geography by travelling through it, rather than being given a complete explanation at the outset. Finding a connection therefore provides two rewards: an easier return route and a clearer understanding of the world. Repeated journeys become less uncertain as familiar landmarks and newly opened paths turn a confusing territory into a place the player can navigate.

cards.heading: Stamina and the choice of weapon
cards.text: Attacking, blocking a blow, sprinting and dodging draw on stamina, so a fight requires pauses as well as action. An extra blow can leave too little energy to defend or escape. Weapon choice adds another decision: reach, attack speed and animations matter alongside damage. Miyazaki explained that a player might prefer a familiar sword to a more powerful weapon that behaves differently. Fighting with two weapons is possible, but giving up a shield also means losing its protection. Learning when to attack, recover and change equipment is as important as improving statistics.

cards.heading: Bonfires and another attempt
cards.text: Bonfires restore the player and provide recovery points after death. Resting also brings many enemies back, so safety comes with the need to cross part of the route again. Familiarity makes these journeys more manageable: the player knows where danger waits and can reconsider the approach. Miyazaki wanted death to leave room for a new strategy, not merely another repetition of the same actions. A different route, weapon or attack timing may change the outcome. Bonfires give this cycle a rhythm, offering relief without removing the danger of the surrounding world.

cards.heading: Other players in a solitary journey
cards.text: Online encounters are woven into individual exploration. Messages and traces suggest that other people have passed through the same places; summoning allows cooperation, while invasions bring conflict. Miyazaki described a multiplayer system surrounding the single-player journey, with players crossing paths according to their circumstances and aims. Lordran does not become a conventional shared world with continuous conversation. Instead, its often anonymous and intermittent encounters make solitude less absolute: another player may briefly offer help, a warning or a new threat before the journey continues.

main.title: The Binding of Isaac
main.subtitle: A changing basement and an unsettling childhood nightmare
main.summary: Edmund McMillen and Florian Himsl’s original 2011 game combines room-based action, randomly generated dungeons and items that transform Isaac. Its Flash origins and Danny Baranowsky score distinguish it from the later Rebirth remake.

cards.heading: A frightened child escapes into the basement
cards.text: The Binding of Isaac was released for Windows on 28 September 2011. Designed by Edmund McMillen and Florian Himsl, it follows a child fleeing into his basement after his mother believes she has been ordered to sacrifice him. Its grotesque cartoon world turns that escape into an action adventure through rooms filled with monsters, secrets and bosses.

cards.heading: Every run rearranges the dungeon
cards.text: The dungeon changes from one run to the next. Players move between connected rooms, defeat enemies in real time and search for a route to the floor’s boss. Isaac fires tears as projectiles and can use a limited supply of bombs. Losing all his hearts ends the run: the next attempt begins in a newly generated dungeon rather than simply continuing from the same room.

cards.heading: Items change Isaac and his attacks
cards.text: Treasures do more than improve a number on a status screen. Items can visibly alter Isaac, strengthen his tears or change how he attacks, and their effects can combine. Passive upgrades, reusable active items and single-use consumables create different decisions. Coins pay for shop purchases, while keys open special rooms, making exploration and the resources carried through a run closely connected.

cards.heading: The Flash original and its later remake
cards.text: The project grew from a prototype created by McMillen and Himsl during a short game jam and was built in Adobe Flash. Danny Baranowsky composed its original soundtrack. Wrath of the Lamb expanded this game in 2012, while Nicalis developed the separate remake The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth, released in 2014 with new graphics and technology that overcame Flash’s limits. The original and Rebirth therefore represent different editions of Isaac’s history.

main.title: Rage
main.summary: Rage is a first-person shooter video game developed by id Software and published by Bethesda Softworks, released in October 2011 for Microsoft Windows, the PlayStation 3, and the Xbox 360, and in February 2012 for OS X.

cards.heading: An id Tech 5 shooter follows a 2007 demo
cards.text: Rage is a first-person shooter video game developed by id Software and published by Bethesda Softworks, released in October 2011 for Microsoft Windows, the PlayStation 3, and the Xbox 360, and in February 2012 for OS X. It was first shown as a tech demo at the 2007 Apple Worldwide Developers Conference and was announced at the QuakeCon. Rage uses id Software's id Tech 5 game engine and is the final game released by the company under the supervision of founder John Carmack.

cards.heading: Nicholas Raine awakens a century later
cards.text: Rage is set in a post-apocalyptic near future, following the impact of the asteroid 99942 Apophis on Earth. Players take control of Nicholas Raine, a soldier put into hibernation in an underground shelter who emerges into the wasteland a century later, and finds himself a wanted man by an oppressive organization known as The Authority. The game has been described as similar to the movie Mad Max 2, and video games such as Duke Nukem, Fallout and Borderlands.

cards.heading: Praised combat, criticised story and a sequel
cards.text: Rage received mainly positive reviews, with reviewers praising the game's combat mechanics, gameplay and graphics while criticizing the lack of story, characters, and direction. A sequel, Rage 2, was released on May 14, 2019.

main.title: Pushmo
main.subtitle: Pull a picture into a staircase
main.summary: Pushmo is Intelligent Systems' Nintendo 3DS puzzle game about rescuing children trapped in large structures made from sliding blocks. Known as Pullblox in Europe, it stars Mallo, a small red character who can push and pull sections of a colourful design to make a climbable route. A picture that first looks flat becomes a set of platforms with different depths. The goal is visible, but reaching it requires changing the structure beneath it. The puzzle is both an image to understand and a space that must support Mallo's next jump.

cards.heading: Pull a picture into a staircase
cards.text: Pushmo is Intelligent Systems' Nintendo 3DS puzzle game about rescuing children trapped in large structures made from sliding blocks. Known as Pullblox in Europe, it stars Mallo, a small red character who can push and pull sections of a colourful design to make a climbable route. A picture that first looks flat becomes a set of platforms with different depths. The goal is visible, but reaching it requires changing the structure beneath it. The puzzle is both an image to understand and a space that must support Mallo's next jump.

cards.heading: Make room for the next step
cards.text: Pulling one block creates a ledge, but the position of neighbouring pieces determines whether that ledge can actually be reached. Mallo must stand in the right place to manipulate a section, so a solution includes the route taken while constructing it. The player learns to consider depth as well as height. A promising arrangement can leave no room for the next action, requiring another approach. The tactile rhythm of pull, climb and inspect makes a compact set of movements capable of supporting increasingly elaborate spatial problems.

cards.heading: A small rescue gives the puzzle a face
cards.text: Pushmo Park supplies a friendly setting for these structures, with Papa Blox introducing the play area and the trapped children providing a clear destination. The characters make the objective understandable before the arrangement becomes complicated. Each rescue is a complete little journey from the ground to the point inside the design where somebody is waiting. The stereoscopic display suits that journey by making the separate depths easy to inspect. Pushmo finds personality in a practical act: reshaping a playful object until another person can be reached.

main.title: Forza Motorsport 4
main.summary: Forza Motorsport 4 is a 2011 racing video game developed by Turn 10 Studios and published by Microsoft Studios for the Xbox 360.

cards.heading: Forza meets Kinect
cards.text: Forza Motorsport 4 is a 2011 racing video game developed by Turn 10 Studios and published by Microsoft Studios for the Xbox 360. It is the fourth installment in the Forza series. It is the first title in the series to support the Kinect sensor alongside the traditional controller-based gameplay. It is the last Forza Motorsport released for Xbox 360; 2012's Forza Horizon and its 2014 sequel were the last two Forza games for the platform, while 2013's Forza Motorsport 5 was released as an Xbox One exclusive.

cards.heading: Autovista, Top Gear and over 500 cars
cards.text: A new feature in the series is Autovista, a game mode in which players can view precise details such as engine parts and interior gauges on a select number of cars. It features a partnership with BBC's Top Gear as well as its American counterpart. Jeremy Clarkson, then-presenter for Top Gear, provided commentary in the game's Autovista mode. Other partnerships include a two-year agreement with the American Le Mans Series (ALMS). Over 500 cars and 26 tracks are included.

cards.heading: Physics and sound win critical praise
cards.text: The game received universal acclaim from critics, who praised the enhanced vehicle physics, updated visuals, and strong sound design. Several reviewers also gave high marks for the game's Autovista mode. Some critics expressed frustration with Kinect features, and others also felt that the game was not enough of an innovation from its predecessor, Forza Motorsport 3. These critics did, however, concede that the game was a vast improvement over Forza Motorsport 3.

main.title: Batman: Arkham City
main.subtitle: Batman in a prison city
main.summary: Batman explores an urban prison through gliding, investigation, combat and stealth in Rocksteady's 2011 sequel to Arkham Asylum.

cards.heading: Bruce Wayne inside the prison city
cards.text: Batman: Arkham City is a 2011 action-adventure game developed by Rocksteady Studios and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment. Based on the DC Comics superhero Batman, it is the sequel to the 2009 video game Batman: Arkham Asylum and the second installment in the Batman: Arkham series. Written by veteran Batman writer Paul Dini with Paul Crocker and Sefton Hill, Arkham City was inspired by the long-running comic book mythos. In the game's main storyline, Bruce Wayne is incarcerated in Arkham City, a super-prison enclosing the decaying urban slums of Gotham City. He dons his alter ego, Batman, and goes on a mission to uncover the secret behind a sinister scheme orchestrated by the facility's warden, Hugo Strange.

cards.heading: Exploration, gadgets and Catwoman
cards.text: The game is presented from the third-person perspective with a primary focus on Batman's combat and stealth abilities, detective skills, and gadgets that can be used in both combat and exploration. Batman can freely move around the Arkham City prison, interacting with characters and undertaking missions, and unlocking new areas by progressing through the main story or obtaining new equipment. The player is able to complete side missions away from the main story to unlock additional content and collectible items. Batman's ally Catwoman is another playable character, featuring her own story campaign that runs parallel to the game's main plot.

cards.heading: Freeflow, Predator and Detective Mode
cards.text: Freeflow combat asks the player to respond to different enemies: countering, disarming, stunning or choosing a suitable gadget. Reading the group and maintaining position matter more than memorizing long combinations. In Predator encounters, gargoyles, grates and fragile walls offer ways to separate armed guards and strike without becoming a fixed target. Takedowns make the remaining guards more nervous and change their behavior. Detective Mode complements both exploration and investigation by highlighting people, interactive objects and useful information. Together, these systems let Batman alternate between direct combat, observation and prepared ambushes.

cards.heading: Building a city for Batman to glide through
cards.text: Rocksteady conceived ideas for a sequel while developing Arkham Asylum, commencing serious development of Arkham City's story in February 2009. The layout of Arkham City has a virtual footprint five times that of Arkham Asylum, and the city design was modified to accommodate Batman's ability to swoop and glide. Over a year and $10 million were spent on the game's marketing campaign, and its release was accompanied by two music albums; one containing the game's score, and the other featuring 11 original songs inspired by the game from various mainstream artists.

cards.heading: Critical acclaim in 2011
cards.text: Arkham City was released worldwide for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 video game consoles in October 2011, followed by a Microsoft Windows version a month later. The game received critical acclaim, particularly for its narrative, characters, world design, soundtrack, and Batman's combat and navigation abilities. It was tied with The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim for the highest-rated video game of 2011 according to review aggregator Metacritic, and was the recipient of several awards from media outlets, including Game of the Year, Best Action Game, Best Action Adventure Game, Best Adventure Game, and Best Original Score. Like its predecessor, it is considered one of the greatest video games ever made.

cards.heading: New editions and the Arkham series
cards.text: A spin-off mobile game, Batman: Arkham City Lockdown, was released in December. Arkham City received a "Game of the Year Edition" in May 2012. Wii U and OS X versions of the game were released in November and December 2012, respectively; and a remastered version for the PlayStation 4 and Xbox One in October 2016. A version for the Nintendo Switch was released in 2023. A prequel to the series, Batman: Arkham Origins, was released in October 2013, and a narrative sequel, Batman: Arkham Knight, was released in June 2015.

main.title: Rocksmith
main.subtitle: A real guitar at the console
main.summary: Rocksmith, developed by Ubisoft San Francisco and published by Ubisoft, reached North American consoles in October 2011. Instead of a five-button imitation, it connects an electric guitar with a standard output jack through the Real Tone Cable. The notes come from an instrument the player can continue using away from the screen.

cards.heading: A real guitar at the console
cards.text: Rocksmith, developed by Ubisoft San Francisco and published by Ubisoft, reached North American consoles in October 2011. Instead of a five-button imitation, it connects an electric guitar with a standard output jack through the Real Tone Cable. The notes come from an instrument the player can continue using away from the screen.

cards.heading: Learning through performance
cards.text: A perspective view of the fretboard turns the song into positions, strings and timing. The difficulty adapts to performance, while separate technique exercises and the Guitarcade practise particular skills. The amplifier interface also lets players experiment with virtual equipment and effects, making the guitar more than a controller for a score.

cards.heading: Songs and the original edition
cards.text: Licensed recordings, including Blur’s Song 2, the Black Keys’ Next Girl and Muse’s Plug in Baby, connect practice to familiar music. The original game later expanded to bass and Windows in 2012. Those additions belong to its history; Rocksmith 2014 is a separate successor, not the edition documented here.

main.title: Golden Joystick Awards 2011
main.summary: The Golden Joystick Awards, with every category winner of the 2011 edition.

cards.heading: The players' awards
cards.text: The Golden Joystick Awards celebrate games through a public vote, bringing players into the choice of each year's winners. The awards began in Britain with the 1983 season and later reached an international audience through online voting. Their changing categories trace the growth of games: home computers and consoles, handhelds, online play, independent studios, performance and music. Alongside the public vote, special honours recognise individual contributions to the industry. Each edition preserves its own category names, so the results also show what players and the awards organisers considered worth celebrating at the time.

main.title: Kirby's Return to Dream Land
main.summary: Four players can help rebuild Magolor's ship, combining Kirby's copied powers with huge temporary Super Abilities and a search for hidden Energy Spheres.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Kirby's Return to Dream Land is HAL Laboratory's 2011 Wii platform game, released in Europe as Kirby's Adventure Wii. It brings Kirby's side-scrolling adventures and copied powers to a four-player cooperative game, beginning when Magolor's damaged ship lands on Popstar and scatters its parts across the planet.

cards.heading: Make room for four adventurers
cards.text: Friends can join as other coloured Kirbies or choose King Dedede, Meta Knight and Bandana Waddle Dee, whose weapons give them distinct ways to fight. Everyone shares the scrolling view, so a platform or a boss has to accommodate more than one approach at once. A player can ride on another character, and the group can keep moving together when someone needs help. New players may enter or leave during the adventure, making the expedition easy to continue with a changing group.

cards.heading: A power that changes the scale
cards.text: Kirby's regular Copy Abilities offer different attacks and movement options, while certain glowing enemies provide a temporary Super Ability. These enlarge the effect dramatically: a giant sword can sweep through much of the screen and break scenery along with enemies. The power lasts for a limited time, encouraging the player to use the opening while it is available. Super Inhale provides another change of scale, gathering large objects and several enemies into a star that Kirby can send back across the room.

cards.heading: Find the missing pieces
cards.text: Repairing Magolor's ship gives the journey its route, with major parts recovered after the larger confrontations. Hidden Energy Spheres add smaller tasks within the stages. Some lie behind an ability puzzle; others lead through another dimension, where a moving wall makes exploration more urgent. Collected spheres open additional activities aboard the ship, including ability challenges. Returning with the right power can therefore reward a careful search even after a stage has already helped restore the Lor Starcutter.
